content: LVCT Health provides critical services outside traditional healthcare settings and schedules to address barriers faced by key populations in accessing consistent care. Their programs are peer-led and involve meaningful community engagement throughout all stages of the program cycle. To effectively target interventions, hotspots were mapped in collaboration with community leaders and service providers, who were trained to deliver non-judgmental and appropriate services. Focus group discussions and client exit interviews with key population groups informed the design of innovative programs. Partnerships with bar owners and staff facilitated the availability of condoms and lubricants in accessible dispensers. Clients diagnosed with HIV through LVCT Health’s testing services are promptly linked to treatment and care. Data on HIV risk factors, STI types, and HIV status are entered into a national database, and cohort data is analyzed for trends, such as HIV prevalence by geographic location. Female sex workers receive routine STI and cervical cancer screenings using visual methods, with immediate diagnoses provided and referrals made for further management of lesions. Male sex workers are screened for STIs and other lesions, offered on-site syndromic management, and followed up in facility settings. LVCT Health reaches approximately 5,000 key population clients annually with HIV and sexual and reproductive health services, with over 80% of HIV-positive clients effectively linked to post-test services. The organization has achieved over 85% retention in care and treatment for men who have sex with men (MSM) and over 90% adherence to antiretroviral therapy (HAART). LVCT Health’s advocacy has led to the inclusion of key population issues in Kenya’s HIV National Strategic Plan, paving the way for national scale-up of services. Consistent follow-up with mobile populations is conducted through telephone calls by counselors and a static site near hotspots for follow-up services or unscheduled appointments. The National Organization of Peer Educators (NOPE) provides sexual and reproductive health and social services in diverse settings. NOPE developed the Drop-In Service Centre (DiSC) model as a “one-stop” approach for delivering essential HIV services to female sex workers (FSWs) and MSM in Kisii and Kiambu counties. Consultations and focus group discussions with FSW and MSM community members identified service gaps, followed by social and hotspot mapping and population size estimations. Stakeholder meetings, including bar owners, police, administrators, religious leaders, and community representatives, were held to provide project information and encourage community buy-in. FSWs and MSM participated in selecting DiSC locations, and peer educators were trained to manage the centers, including setting them up, using client flowcharts, and ensuring a minimum service package. A performance-monitoring plan aligned with the national AIDS strategic plan and PEPFAR indicators is followed, with routine data quality assessments, audits, supervision visits, and data-sharing forums ensuring robust monitoring and evaluation. DiSCs have served 20,000 individuals from FSW and MSM communities. Based on their experiences, NOPE has contributed to national guidelines for key populations and developed a national MSM peer education curriculum. Technical assistance from NOPE has enabled other organizations, such as Ishtar MSM and Keeping Alive Societies’ Hope, to take over three DiSCs. A key lesson from establishing DiSCs is the importance of gaining the trust of key populations, especially in environments where laws and policies criminalize their behaviors. While standalone facilities are critical, sustainability will require integrating services for these groups into national health systems as communities and providers become more responsive to their needs. In the meantime, NOPE has successfully mobilized county health management teams to provide medical supplies and second medical staff to DiSCs. The Marsa Sexual Health Centre in Beirut offers sexual and reproductive health services in a welcoming, stigma-free environment, targeting young people, unmarried sexually active women, and marginalized communities, including MSM and transgender individuals. Anonymity and confidentiality are prioritized, with clients assigned unique file numbers and deciding whether to provide additional identifying information. Marsa does not advertise publicly but uses social media, the internet, street outreach campaigns, and word-of-mouth to share information about its services. Médecins du Monde (MdM) implements a program in Myanmar focused on STI and HIV prevention, treatment, care, and harm reduction for FSWs, MSM, and people who use drugs. Services are provided free of charge at drop-in centers and clinics, developed in collaboration with key populations. Education, information, and supplies build trust, encouraging individuals to visit facilities for more services. Strong relationships with local authorities influence operational frameworks and promote evidence-based policies. While HIV prevalence among key populations has decreased in Myanmar, addressing basic health needs alongside harm reduction is essential for program acceptance and reducing misunderstandings. The Naz Male Health Alliance (NMHA) in Pakistan addresses the health and psychosocial needs of young males who have sex with males and transgender individuals. Operating six service delivery centers in five cities, NMHA serves 47,000 registered clients. Each site includes a clinic and a drop-in center, providing a safe space for low-income MSM and transgender clients. Centers are strategically located near community hotspots and “hijra deras” (transgender dwellings). Services include STI treatment, psychosocial support, and harm reduction education. Over 95% of staff are community members, fostering trust and engagement. NMHA has significantly increased HIV diagnoses among MSM and transgender individuals in public treatment centers and collaborates with national and international organizations to strengthen its impact. In South Africa, a multi-partner project led by SANAC and the Department of Health trains healthcare providers to address key population issues and interact appropriately with these communities. Training sessions have improved healthcare workers’ attitudes, increased community trust, and enhanced the use of health facilities. Further evaluation is planned to inform scale-up. Kimara Peers, a community-based NGO in Tanzania, operates two drop-in centers near state-run health facilities to serve people who use drugs, including young individuals aged 16–24. Services include psychosocial therapy, harm reduction education, and referrals for methadone therapy and STI treatment. Confidentiality is maintained, and referrals to government hospitals are made only with the client’s consent. The program seeks government approval to provide clean needles and syringes. Save the Children uses information and communication technologies (ICT) to enhance HIV prevention outreach to MSM and transgender individuals in Chiang Mai, Thailand. The project leverages social media platforms popular among these communities to provide HIV-related information and engage users. Outreach workers use tablets to share content, record contact details, and promote free HIV testing. Continued online contact builds trust and encourages service uptake. The New York State Department of Health’s “Test, Connect & Treat” program targets high-risk adolescents and young adults for HIV testing, linking HIV-positive individuals to care and providing prevention information to HIV-negative individuals. Services are offered through 14 Specialized Care Centers with multidisciplinary teams providing comprehensive care. Case management focuses on strengths and self-management skills, addressing barriers such as mental health and substance abuse issues. Globally, numerous programs address the needs of key populations often excluded from formal health systems. The featured interventions highlight innovative approaches and the importance of critical enablers in delivering services to key populations. While challenges remain, these programs inspire further efforts to expand and sustain this vital work.
